title: Prendergast cited and could miss South Africa game
article_text:
Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast is in danger of missing Saturday's Nations Championship match against South Africa after being cited for a tackle against Fiji.

Prendergast will face a disciplinary process for a hip-drop tackle on Fijian captain Peceli Yato in the first half of Ireland's 43-15 win in Dublin on Saturday.

The technique, when a tackling player drops their hips and bodyweight on to the ball-carrier's legs, was outlawed by World Rugby before November's internationals and the 23-year-old is the first player to be cited over its use in a game.

If found guilty and he accepts the verdict, Prendergast could face a pre-determined sanction through the Six Nations' expedited disciplinary process.

However, if he does not accept the charge then he would be referred to a panel to determine any possible outcome.

Australia's Angus Bell was yellow carded for a hip-drop tackle against England, but Prendergast's alleged offence was not penalised by match officials during the match.

If Prendergast receives a suspension, Connacht fly-half Ciaran Frawley would be the prime candidate to start against the Springboks on Saturday [16:40 GMT].

Ulster's Jamie Benson, who has yet to be capped at international level, is also an option for Farrell.

In better news for Ireland, captain Dan Sheehan is set to return for the game against the back-to-back world champions at the Aviva Stadium after he completed return to play protocols.

Sheehan - who is deputising for regular skipper Caelan Doris - missed Saturday's win over Fiji after sustaining a concussion in the defeat of Argentina on 6 November.

But in a squad update issued on Monday, the Irish Rugby Football Union (IRFU) said Sheehan will return to full training this week before the Springboks' visit to Dublin.

Ulster back row James McNabney is unavailable while he undergoes 12-day return to play protocols after sustaining a head injury that prematurely ended his eye-catching debut off the bench against the Fijians.

Tight-head prop Sam Illo is a doubt as he enters the return to play process, while utility back Jamie Osborne is ruled out with a pectoral injury that forced him off in the opening minutes of the Fiji game.

If Illo misses the Springboks game, Farrell has Thomas Clarkson and Tom O'Toole as back-up tight-head options with Tadhg Furlong expected to start.

Farrell will name his team to face the back-to-back world champions at 14:00 GMT on Thursday.

South Africa won last year's meeting 24-13 in Dublin but lost to France in Paris last weekend.

title: Harlequins land highly rated Eagles playmaker for new PWR campaign
article_text:
USA Women’s Eagles back Nina Mason has signed for Harlequins for the 2026/27 JAECOO Premiership Women’s Rugby campaign.

Mason made her Test debut for the Eagles in September, as the USA completed a 19-point turnaround to win in Dublin, and then started four international fixtures in a row to conclude WXV Global Series.

Two of those starts resulted in back-to-back victories against Italy in Texas and Tennessee. Mason also started in the Eagles’ 55-12 loss to the Red Roses at the end of October.

Mason said: “I’m so excited for the opportunity to experience rugby in England and be a part of such a great team. I’m looking forward to this next chapter with Harlequins Women and linking up with such a talented squad of players.”

Mason arrives in West London as a highly regarded prospect. During her time at Life University she was a standout performer as the team won the CRAA Division I 15s title and USA Rugby Division I Club 15s National Championship in 2026. In April, the team also won the CRAA Premier Division 7s National Championship.

Capable of playing fly-half or centre, Mason forged a formidable midfield partnership with World Rugby Women’s 15s Breakthrough Player of the Year nominee and university teammate Bella Vogel in WXV Global Series.

She is the latest arrival at the Twickenham Stoop, who have also recruited England internationals Marlie Packer and Rosie Galligan, along with Wales’ Sisilia Tuipulotu and Italy’s Sara Mannini.

Ross Chisholm, Harlequins head coach, said: “We’re excited for Nina to join us here at Harlequins. She can play in multiple positions across the backline and has shown a lot of promise in the recent WXV Series for the USA.

“She is a player who has a great feel for the game and ability to play in a number of different ways.

“She is a young player with a lot of talent and we’re looking forward to seeing what she can bring to our environment.”

title: Wales international steps away from rugby at 29 in 'difficult' announcement
article_text:
Wales international Alisha Joyce has announced she is taking a break from rugby after more than a decade representing her country, with the 29-year-old deciding to step away as she reassesses her priorities.

The flanker, who won 54 caps for Wales, has informed the Welsh Rugby Union of her decision, which has been accepted by the governing body as she takes stock of her future.

Joyce has been a mainstay of the Wales squad since making her international debut against Ireland in the 2016 Six Nations and became one of the most recognisable faces in the women's game.

Her decision comes less than a year after one of the most remarkable chapters of her career, having returned to international rugby just 158 days after giving birth to her son Ralphie in November 2025.

Married to fellow Wales international Jasmine Joyce, Alisha had initially stepped away during her pregnancy but made her return to rugby after just 123 days, coming off the bench for Brython Thunder in the Celtic Challenge semi-finals.

She subsequently earned a place on the bench for Wales' clash with England in the 2026 Women's Six Nations, with her return to Test rugby becoming one of the standout stories of the championship.

Alongside her wife Jaz, she also helped document their journey into parenthood through the Vodafone-backed 'Still a Force' docuseries, which followed their decision to start a family through IVF. The series won Best Brand Partnership in Women's Sport at the 2026 ISC Awards.

In a statement, Joyce said: "This has been a difficult decision but one I have been contemplating for a while. I have loved being a professional rugby player and I wouldn’t have missed it for the world.

"It just feels like the right time to step away with my priorities having changed and having played rugby at the highest level for more than a decade.

"I always intended to return and resume my rugby career when I was first pregnant, and I am proud that I did that and hope it proves that it can be done.

"Playing for Wales has been a privilege and being part of the revolution in women’s rugby and seeing it grow as fast as it has, is something I am proud to have played a part in.

"I would like to thank everyone, teammates, coaches and staff at the WRU for the support I’ve had during my pregnancy and since being a mum and as a professional rugby player."

Wales head coach Sean Lynn paid tribute to Joyce's contribution, while making clear she would be welcome back in the international set-up.

"Alisha has been one of the most recognisable faces in women’s rugby and will be missed by her teammates, coaches and staff in the Wales set-up.

"They way she returned to Test match rugby 158 days after giving birth to Ralphie was truly inspirational to everyone.

"We respect ‘Butch’s’ decision but hope she knows the door is always open and do hope she stays involved in the game in some capacity."

WRU director of rugby and elite performance Dave Reddin added: "We all respect Alisha’s decision and appreciate how tough it would have been to make this decision.

"She has been a key figure in the Wales squad and very much a face of women’s rugby in Wales and we wish her all the best in the future."

WRU director of women's rugby Nadine Griffiths described Joyce as an inspiration to the next generation.

"Alisha has been such an inspiration to so many people as a player and a person, and I had the honour of seeing the impact she has had when I picked up the award for the docuseries ‘Still a Force’ on her and Jaz’s behalf.

"She will be one of the Welsh players who young players will reference as their hero and inspiration and will acknowledge as one of the giants of the game who showed them what can be achieved."

title: New World Rugby rankings published as Wales save Springboks in dramatic 18 hours
article_text:
Wales' historic victory over New Zealand has seen them move up to ninth in the world rankings and had a huge impact at the very top of the global order after a dramatic 18 hours.

The 35-28 win over the All Blacks also saw world champions South Africa regain first place after they had temporarily dropped to second following their 21-19 defeat by France in Paris on Friday night. It also resurrected the Springboks' hopes of winning the Nations Championship after they thought it was over for them.

Wales gained the highest amount of rankings points on the weekend (+2.00) and will rise further up the rankings if they can beat Australia at the Principality Stadium this Saturday.

France also moved into the top three in the world rankings following their stunning victory on Friday night with New Zealand in second place.

Despite Ireland's 43-15 hammering of Fiji at the Aviva Stadium on Saturday night, Ireland drop down to fourth place behind France.

Defeat for Fiji saw them overtaken by Wales and Jake White's side now sit in tenth place.

France are now very close to the top two on 89.09 points with New Zealand on 90.65 and South Africa on 91.53 in first place.

Scotland's narrow 15-12 win over Australia at Murrayfield on Sunday saw Gregor Townsend's men gain 0.87 ranking points but they remain in sixth place with the Wallabies in seventh.

Argentina gained 0.47 points after their 19-14 win over Italy but they remain in eight place one position above Wales.

The Azzurri have dropped out of the top 10 to 11th place.

title: Brady Rush hopes to bring Northland’s fairytale NPC success to SVNS
article_text:
All Blacks Sevens veteran Brady Rush is hoping to transfer Northland’s NPC success into the upcoming 2026/2027 HSBC SVNS Series.

Northland were the fairytale of the 50th NPC, winning the Ranfurly Shield for the first time since 1979 and later making their first final. They led 21-10 at halftime before succumbing to defending champions and 16-time winners Canterbury in Christchurch.

Rush started 10 games on the wing and scored four tries. Two came in a 40-14 win against Manawatu, and the others in the successful 34-17 defence of the Ranfurly Shield against Waikato and the 26-21 quarter-final victory against Tasman.

“It still feels a little surreal, what we’ve done,” Rush told RugbyPass.

“It was special for the community to come together as it did. We hadn’t won the Shield since the days of the Going brothers. Seeing what that win meant to that generation, and inspiring a new generation, are forever memories.

“After we beat Canterbury to win the Shield, the airport was packed out. Then we went on a road trip where we were treated like rockstars.

“We’ve been building over the last couple of years with a core group of boys and growing ambition. Ryan Martin is a bloody wizard, bro. Coming up North and embracing the culture and community straight away won the boys’ respect. As a coach, his detail and knowledge are second to none. Add legends Ross Wright and Robbie Abel, and from the first camp I thought, Bro, this is going to be a pretty cool season.”

Northland’s 36-12 dismantling of Canterbury on August 20 was their first win over Canterbury since 1999 and their first in Christchurch since 1987. Canterbury also suffered their heaviest home defeat since 2014. Brady’s brother Rob Rush scored two tries. He’s recovering strongly from a knee injury.

Northland repelled Shield challenges from Tasman (20-10) and Waikato (34-17) before losing to 13th-placed Counties Manukau 22-19 in their last home game of the regular season. It was a setback that could have derailed their season but instead had a mobilising effect.

“We didn’t take our chances in the Counties game, but it was cool to see a small Union like them win. Similar to us, they had parades, a packed stadium and an awesome buzz,” Rush said.

“Our goal at the start of the season was to make the final and win it. The Shield was a bonus. When we lost the Shield, it was easy to bounce back. We had a chip on our shoulder and bigger fish to fry.”

Northland rallied to beat Southland (28-14), Tasman (26-21) and Otago (38-19) to make the NPC final against Canterbury. Rush rues the defeat to the 43-24 defeat in the decider.

“It was going so well at halftime. Canterbury are a bloody good team and showed it on the day. Once they got momentum, the crowd got stuck in and they were hard to stop. I can’t put my finger on a single moment we lost, just a culmination of small moments.”

The All Blacks Sevens experienced a similar rollercoaster of emotions in HSBC SVNS 2025/2026. After winning the Dubai Sevens first up, they failed to win another title, slipping to fourth in the league standings.

In the trilogy of Grand Final tournaments, New Zealand lifted to second, narrowly losing a Cup final thriller to hosts France in Bordeaux.

“It’s a hard comp, eight teams. Anyone can beat anyone on their day,” Rush said.

“We had a lot of injuries last year that didn’t help, but we definitely changed a few things at home around preparation that helped us improve. Young fellas like Riely Williams, Fletcher Morgan and Jayden Keelan really grew during the season.

“This year is a fresh start. We’ve got a new coaching group and promising young players coming through like Grady Forbes and Nathan Salmon from Northland. Hopefully they can bring some of the Taniwha buzz.”

This weekend at the Ignite Sevens in Mount Maunganui, a New Zealand Development side that will make up most of the All Blacks Sevens had a three-match series with Samoa and Fiji.

Two tries from Brayden Neilson secured an initial 12-12 draw against Fiji, who were then beaten 12-7 and 7-5 in the next two games. Sprightly Jayden Keelan scored a crucial try in each contest.

Northland duo Scott Gregory and Nathan Salmon scored in a first-up 14-5 win against Samoa, which improved to 31-5 in the next match, with Keelan again among the scorers alongside stalwarts Regan Ware and Andrew Knewstubb.

Samoa would have the last say with a 24-17 win. Beast Taunuu Niulevaea was a handful with two tries. Salmon, Riley Williams and Joe Webber scored for New Zealand.

The Emirates Dubai 7s 2026 takes place from November 27–29 at The Sevens Stadium in Dubai. New Zealand have won the cup title six times. The current league and Grand Final champions, South Africa, are the most prolific winners, with 11 titles since 1999.

title: Townsend hails Scotland's defence in Australia 'arm wrestle'
article_text:
Scotland head coach Gregor Townsend hailed his team's defensive efforts after they edged past Australia in a Nations Championship "arm wrestle" at Murrayfield.

Off the back of being dismantled by New Zealand last weekend, in which they failed to score a second half point, the spotlight fell on Scotland's leaky defence.

But on a chilly and damp Edinburgh day where physicality was king, they delivered a much-needed win and showed they are capable of winning ugly.

Even so, Townsend's side didn't make it easy.

Max Jorgensen's late converted try gave the Wallabies hope, and with the clock in the red, the visitors broke from their own half.

Murrayfield held its breath, but Darcy Graham hauled Australia full-back Tom Wright into touch with a superb tackle.

"When we saw the rain half an hour before kick-off, you still hope you'll be able to move the ball," Townsend said.

"You could tell defences were coming off the line a bit quicker, knowing they could pressure the ball carrier.

"Both teams had to adjust and I thought we did that well. Defensively, that's one of the best performances I've seen in the last couple of years. Set after set we were putting them under pressure.

"We were on that edge of physicality but disciplined, hitting hard in the tackle, putting pressure on, listening to the referee, getting back onside. That makes it hard for the opposition to get into our 22m, which was a learning from last week.

"It was just constant effort. Today, we showed we can play another game, too."

Leading 12-5 at half-time, there was one eye on whether Scotland could clinch a bonus-point victory that would have both boosted their points difference and helped their chances of climbing the northern hemisphere table with Japan to come on Saturday.

However, it soon became apparent that would not be forthcoming in a match that will not live long in the memory.

"It was about winning at all costs today," former Scotland prop Peter Wright said.

"We hoped we might get something quite end-to-end, 50 points to 48, loads of tries, but to come out on the right end of a war of attrition like that, it's a good feeling.

"When you're Scottish, winning's always good. We very rarely win in style at any sport. We just want to get victories under our belt.

"It was a bad game last week so getting some momentum going into the Japan game next week was really important.

In the absence of Sione Tuipulotu, who was ruled out of playing against the country of his birth with a knee injury, Rory Darge captained Scotland and led from the front with a player-of-the-match display.

The Glasgow Warriors flanker was immense in contact and at the breakdown, and also had the presence of mind to tell Finn Russell to kick at goal instead of going to the corner in the closing stages.

The resulting three points put Scotland 10 points in front and proved to be the winning score.

Townsend praised the performance his stand-in skipper, while also pointing to a wider effort defensively.

"You know the opposition will get phases of attack and we'll have to defend. Rory with his tackling, with his effort and his post-tackle presence really helps us.

"There were a lot of other players that stood up physically. The shots that were going in, the effort going in was outstanding."

And Darge himself was heartened by how Scotland responded to the All Blacks loss.

"We were disappointed after last week's performance," he said.

"A lot of that disappointment was with the physical side of the game and we did that really well.

"It was a bit of an arm wrestle, the conditions played their part. We know they want to throw the ball around, we like to play an attacking style but today was a battle of the defences."

title: WTA chair Camillo points to 'commercial growth and new alliances'
WTA chair Valerie Camillo says the Jessica Pegula-Mirra Andreeva incident at Indian Wells was 'not bad for viewership'
article_text:
WTA chief Valerie Camillo says private comments made by Jessica Pegula about Mirra Andreeva being overheard on a YouTube livestream is "not bad for viewership".

Camillo personally apologised to Pegula, describing the broadcast of on-court conversations during a practice session at the WTA Finals in Indian Wells as "regrettable and unacceptable".

The Tour, who operated the livestream, had intended for the microphones to capture ambient sounds from the court but failed to inform participants.

A broadcast showed the American in conversation with her coach Mark Knowles, calling the 19-year-old a "diva" and saying she has lost respect for Andreeva's coach Conchita Martinez for not calling out her behaviour.

"Someone actually asked me if we planned it or did it on purpose to draw attention to the event," Camillo told Sky Sports' lead tennis commentator, Jonathan Overend.

"I wish that we were so crafty and strategic but we can't put ourselves in any situation where we put our athletes at risk. Our number one objective as a member services organisation for our players is to protect our players.

"What Jess said is competitive banter. I don't think there was anything particularly salacious in it. But having mics lying around that aren't being properly managed is not how the WTA expects to execute and operate.

"It created a viral moment. It created a lot of dialogue. But that's not intentional and not something you should expect to see us doing in the future.

"I've had this conversation here that I come from a variety of different sports. Before joining the WTA, I exclusively worked in male sports. I worked at the NBA and majorly baseball and it's quite common for there to be competitive banter that is brought into the forefront.

"It's up to the athletes for what they feel comfortable with and what they don't. But a little drama isn't bad for ticket sales.

"It's not bad for viewership. It's not bad for commentary. That's just a reality."

Andreeva laughed off the hot mic moment and went on to defeat Pegula 6-3 6-4 on Saturday, in a match that gained an extra layer of intrigue to reach the WTA Finals title match.

She concluded a stunning week with a second victory over Elina Svitolina to win the season-ending tournament.

The WTA was forced to replace the venue for the season-ending event from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in July, which represented a major financial setback for the governing body.

The deal with the Saudi Tennis Federation (STF) included record prize money over a three-year period, but the ongoing tension between Iran and the United States made planning for the Finals more challenging, eventually forcing the tournament to move to Indian Wells in California.

The body is projecting operating losses of £17.3m ($23m) for 2026 and expects to hold roughly £11.3m ($15m) in cash by the end of the year, according to The Telegraph. Camillo remains confident of finding extra revenue streams through in-house media rights and sponsorship growth to create financial stability.

"Our ambition for the WTA Finals is equal prize money [with the men's tour]. That's our ambition, just as we expected of the Grand Slams. All of our combined 1000 events will have equal prize money in 2027," she said.

"We've been building fandom. We've been operating globally. We've been creating superstar athletes through our platform for many, many decades, and so the athletes have the opportunity not to just earn on the court, but also to control their own brands and monetise that off the court.

"WTA intends to remain in its position as number one in the hearts and minds of fans, in the mindset and investment of our sponsors, and we want to be building an even greater platform on which our great athletes can compete, not only one that they can enjoy from the ferocity of the crowd, but also one that enables them to maximise their financial opportunity to the best of our ability."

One of the WTA revenue streams comes from selling data, match data, court feeds to data companies with the betting industry a large part of that.

British tennis star Jodie Burrage called on social media platforms to hold people accountable for sending death threats and abuse.

Burrage, who was playing her first WTA Tour match since Wimbledon last summer, received death threats and online abuse following a first-round defeat at a tournament in India.

The 27-year-old shared a raft of abusive messages sent to her Instagram account. Alongside the video, Burrage wrote: "Nice welcome back to the tour. I remember why I left."

Camillo said: "The complexity of official data to these partners is sort of an industry inside thing. But the reality is that through having official partnerships, you actually can have more integrity and controls.

"If you don't have relationships with these variety of platforms, you can turn into a little bit of the wild, wild west. It's not to say that there isn't a financial element to these relationships. That would be disingenuous. Of course there is. But it does also enable us to have a partnership that leads to better controls."

title: Rankings Watch: Andreeva ends year at No. 2, Andreescu continues resurgence
article_text:
The 2026 WTA Tour Driven by Mercedes-Benz season concluded last week with the FAGE WTA Finals at Indian Wells, where Mirra Andreeva was crowned champion following a dominant run through the field.

Andreeva, 19, became the youngest WTA Finals champion since a 17-year-old Maria Sharapova in 2004, and the third player in tournament history to lift the trophy on her debut without dropping a set (following Chris Evert in 1972 and Serena Williams in 2001). The 26 games that Andreeva conceded were the second-fewest since 2003, when the event switched to its current round-robin format, behind only Iga Swiatek's 20 games lost in 2023.

As a result, Andreeva climbs one place in the latest edition of the PIF WTA Rankings to end the year at a new career high of No. 2, displacing Aryna Sabalenka to No. 3. This week marks the first time that neither Sabalenka nor Iga Swiatek have featured in the Top 2 since March 2022, when Ashleigh Barty was World No. 1 and Barbora Krejcikova was World No. 2.

The only other movement in the Top 10 as a result of the WTA Finals is semifinalist Linda Noskova's climb of one place to No. 6. The Wimbledon champion ends the year as the Czech No. 1, with Karolina Muchova pushed down one spot to No. 7.

1. Elena Rybakina (+4 from No. 5 in the 2025 year-end rankings)

Last week also saw a number of players use WTA 125 and World Tennis events to put themselves in a strong year-end position.

Former US Open champion Bianca Andreescu claimed the Sopo WTA 125 title on clay in Colombia last week, defeating Elizabeth Mandlik 6-3, 6-3 in the final, to continue her resurgence at that level. In four tournaments across three continents and two surfaces over the past five weeks, the Canadian has reached four finals and collected three trophies, winning 19 of her past 20 matches.

Andreescu ended 2025 ranked No. 227 and five weeks ago, she was at No. 168. She's cut her ranking by 91 spots since then, jumping another 13 places this week from No. 100 to No. 77 -- her highest position since October 2023. Meanwhile, former No. 97 Mandlik climbs 43 places from No. 237 to No. 194 after reaching her second WTA 125 final, and first since Reus 2023.

Three high-level World Tennis tournaments also took place last week. In Brisbane, Joanna Garland collected her second W75 title in the past three months, and moves up 30 spots from No. 182 to No. 152. In Yokohama, Kyoka Okamura lifted the trophy on home soil without dropping a set, and climbs 29 places from No. 243 to No. 214. And in Chihuahua, 2025 finalist Kayla Cross went one better to take the title this year, and advances 15 places from No. 208 to No. 193.

title: Hong Kong Open: Race to Finals Down to the Wire
article_text:
The LI-NING Hong Kong Open 2026 marks the final stop on the HSBC Race to Finals, with the last available points on offer before the HSBC BWF World Tour Finals in Hangzhou next month.

While several berths have already been secured, a handful of coveted spots remain up for grabs across the disciplines, setting the stage for a high-stakes week in Hong Kong.

Among the biggest beneficiaries of late developments is Anders Antonsen. The Dane received a timely boost from the Seed Withdrawal Movement, which elevated him to the No.1 position in the draw in place of top seed Christo Popov. The promotion comes with a first-round bye and, crucially, enough ranking points to mathematically secure his place in Hangzhou.

Not everyone has enjoyed such a fortunate turn; Chinese Taipei’s Chou Tien Chen faces a sterner challenge than originally expected. Scheduled to meet Nhat Nguyen, Chou will instead open against fast-rising Indonesian Moh. Zaki Ubaidillah.

The race could also be influenced by events elsewhere. Following the withdrawal of his original opponent Alwi Farhan, India’s Kidambi Srikanth has an opportunity to help compatriot Lakshya Sen’s hopes when he takes on Koki Watanabe. A Watanabe defeat would secure qualification for Sen, Chou and Kunlavut Vitidsarn, making the first round clash one of the most significant of the week.

The drama is equally intense in the doubles disciplines. In both men’s and women’s doubles, six pairs are vying for four remaining spots, with all contenders present in Hong Kong.

Among those hoping to make history are Lauren Lam and Allison Lee. The duo are chasing a breakthrough qualification that would see them become the first Americans in any doubles discipline to reach a season finale.

With Hangzhou beckoning, the final chapter of the HSBC Race to Finals promises tension, twists and no shortage of drama.

LI-NING Hong Kong Open 2026 begins today, with the first qualification match scheduled for 9am Kuala Lumpur time (UTC +8).

title: Badminton: Aaron-Wooi Yik withdraw from Hong Kong Open, ending World Tour Finals hopes
article_text:
PETALING JAYA: Aaron Chia-Soh Wooi Yik’s bid to reach next month’s World Tour Finals in Hangzhou ended on Monday (Nov 16) when the men’s doubles pair withdrew from the Hong Kong Open.

Hong Kong was the former world champions’ last chance to qualify.

They had been fifth in the qualification standings in October but are projected to slip outside the top eight after the Japan Masters.

Wooi Yik’s right heel injury flared up again in Kumamoto last week, forcing the world No. 4 pair to retire from their opening match against India’s Hariharan Amsakarunan-M. R. Arjun.

The same injury had already kept them out of the Hylo Open and Korean Open.

Fourth seeds Goh Sze Fei-Nur Izzuddin Rumsani also withdrew from the Hong Kong Open, while women’s singles shuttler Goh Jin Wei pulled out with a knee injury.

title: BWF World Ranking: Sindhu Rises To No.5, Lakshya To No.11
article_text:
BWF World Ranking: Sindhu Rises To No.5, Lakshya To No.11

PV Sindhu moves up to world No.5, and Lakshya Sen rises two places to No.11 in the BWF World Rankings in the singles event as the World Tour Finals near.

Indian aces PV Sindhu and Lakshya Sen have moved up in their latest BWF World Rankings. Sindhu has climbed one place to World No.5 in the BWF women’s singles rankings, and Lakshya has climbed two places to No. 11 in the BWF men’s singles rankings. The progress happened after Sen won the Hylo Open and the Kumamoto Masters Japan in two successive weeks, and Sindhu won the Hylo Open 2026. Additionally, Sindhu has already qualified for the World Tour Finals in December, while Lakshya is still in the race for the badminton final tour. In women's doubles, Arjuna Award winners Tressa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand Pullela are currently ranked 19th in the world rankings. The World Championships bronze medallist achieved the highest rank of No.9 in January 2025.

Sindhu was sixth in the badminton rankings on 10 November, so this is her second rise in two weeks. She is also fifth in the World Tour rankings for women’s singles.

Lakshya has beaten Alwi Farhan and Koki Watanabe on his way to the Kumamoto title. He is 5,566 points behind Farhan, who is in tenth.

Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand are 19th with 53,022 points, up one place. They are well behind the fifth-placed Iwanaga and Nakanishi, the Japanese pair who beat them in the Kumamoto Masters Round of 16.

Lakshya won the Kumamoto Masters Japan 2026 title, beating Koki Watanabe 13-21, 21-18, 21-14 in the final. It was his second straight Super 500 title, after the Hylo Open. He is also sixth in the Race to the BWF World Tour Finals, which begins on 9 December in China.

title: Teenager Mirra Andreeva joins elite group of tennis stars after winning WTA Finals without losing a singl
article_text:
NEW DELHI: Russian tennis star Mirra Andreeva capped off a remarkable season by winning the WTA Finals without losing a single set. The 19-year-old defeated Ukraine's Elina Svitolina 7-5, 6-3 in Sunday's final to finish the tournament with five wins from five matches.

The victory also helped Andreeva reach a career-best world ranking of No. 2, behind Kazakhstan's Elena Rybakina.

Along with the title, Andreeva earned $3.37 million in prize money and a unique ultraviolet purple Mercedes-Benz convertible. However, there is one thing she still needs before she can drive her new car: a driver's license.

“This is an amazing motivation for me to get my driver's license as fast as I can,” she said. “If not, then look, I have five people on my team. I'm going to be a passenger's princess forever, that's also an option for me.”

With this victory, Andreeva became only the 11th player to win the WTA Finals without dropping a set. She joined legendary names such as Chris Evert, Martina Navratilova and Serena Williams.

Speaking after her win, the teenager expressed her happiness at joining such an elite group.

“I'm super privileged to put my name in that group,” she said.

Andreeva also took a moment to appreciate her own hard work during the awards ceremony. Wearing a jacket with the words 'I want to thank myself', she spoke about the effort and dedication behind her success.

“I want to thank myself for always doing the hard work, for never quitting, for always believing in myself, for not taking the days off, for working every day and for committing to what I have to do,” she said. “Just thanks to myself without any reason.”

The final was closely fought, with both players exchanging breaks and battling hard from the baseline. However, Andreeva won five of the last six games to seal the title in just under two hours.

The match ended after Svitolina missed an easy smash, giving Andreeva the victory. The players did not shake hands after the match, continuing the practice followed by Ukrainian players against Russian and Belarusian opponents since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Despite the situation, Andreeva congratulated Svitolina on her season and praised her comeback as a mother.

“You're an amazing mom to come back and do this. It's super hard,” she said. “I just wish you the best of luck for the next season.”

Svitolina also acknowledged Andreeva's performance, saying, “I put everything out there and she played incredible.”

title: Siniakova and Townsend win first FAGE WTA Finals title together to cap six-title season

This time, they made it count, defeating Sara Errani and Jasmine Paolini 6-4, 6-3 on Sunday to capture their first FAGE WTA Finals title as a team and their sixth title of the season.

Siniakova and Townsend opened the week with a loss to the Italians in the group stage. Errani and Paolini, the last team to qualify for the season-ending tournament, had won all four of their matches en route to their first WTA Finals championship match. But the second seeds ended that unbeaten run on the same courts where they had won the Indian Wells title in March.

It was Townsend's first WTA Finals title and Siniakova's second, having previously won the championship with Barbora Krejcikova in 2021.

Errani and Paolini made a strong start, securing an early break to take a 3-1 lead in the opening set. But Siniakova and Townsend rallied from 4-2 down, winning four consecutive games to take the set 6-4.

The second set followed a similar pattern, with the Italians breaking serve to go ahead 2-1. However, they were unable to consolidate the break as Siniakova and Townsend broke straight back. The Czech-American duo secured another break in the eighth game before serving out the 6-4, 6-3 victory in 1 hour, 15 minutes.

title: ATP Finals 2026 Day 1 Recap
article_text:
The 2026 ATP Finals got underway in Turin on Sunday, with Alexander Zverev and Ben Shelton both making winning starts in the John McEnroe Group.

World No. 1 Zverev eased past debutant Rafael Jodar in straight sets, while Shelton had to work considerably harder to overcome Arthur Fils in three, recording his first-ever match win at the year-end championships.

Neither match produced a major surprise, but Shelton’s victory sets up a clash with Zverev on Tuesday. Here’s a look at Sunday’s results, match stats and highlights, plus the schedule for Day 2, when Carlos Alcaraz begins his campaign against Frances Tiafoe.

Alexander Zverev (1) def. Rafael Jodar (8) 6-4 6-4

Alexander Zverev got his 2026 ATP Finals campaign off to a winning start on Sunday, defeating debutant Rafael Jodar 6-4, 6-4 in the opening match of the John McEnroe Group.

Zverev has been all over social media again this weekend after his ex-girlfriend filed a new civil lawsuit seeking injunctive monetary relief, claiming he made misleading statements about the legal outcomes of her case against him, which was settled in 2024.

It is, of course, more farcical stuff from Patea, and I am not sure where she got the idea from. Is she skint and needs a new handbag, are lawyers thinking they have a chance to make some cash, or will someone in the tennis article-writing fraternity with an axe to grind have spurred her on?

Back on court, Sascha was largely untroubled by the 20-year-old Spaniard, using his serve and backhand to finish in straight sets.

Jodar put up some resistance early on, saving two break points before Zverev eventually broke at 3-3 with a superb backhand winner down the line.

The German wobbled when serving for the set, falling 15-40 behind, but responded with two aces and two unreturned serves to close it out. His first-serve percentage in the opening set was an impressive 88%, with no double faults.

The second set followed a similar pattern. Jodar showed flashes of the tennis that has propelled him to the season-ending championships, but Zverev was too solid, particularly from the baseline.

Zverev played a businesslike game; his serve clicked, he looked comfortable throughout, and he will be pleased to get his first win on the board without expending too much energy.

Ben Shelton def. Arthur Fils 6-2, 3-6, 6-3

Ben Shelton secured his first-ever ATP Finals match win on Sunday evening, defeating Arthur Fils 6-2, 3-6, 6-3 in a reasonably fun match.

The American raced through the opening set with big hitting from both wings as Fils struggled to get a foothold, with Shelton dominating behind his serve and not facing a single break point.

However, the Frenchman found some success in the second set, extending the rallies and mixing up the pace to disrupt Shelton’s rhythm. He secured the decisive break in the eighth game before saving two break points to serve out the set.

Shelton regained control early in the decider, breaking in the second game to forge a lead he wouldn’t relinquish. He faced one sketchy break point while serving for the match at 5-3, but two huge aces helped him escape trouble before closing out the victory in one hour and 58 minutes.

The match also marked Juan Carlos Ferrero’s first appearance in Shelton’s coaching box, alongside his father Bryan, and I thought Ben played decently, especially on the backhand side for a change. Fils too played one of his better matches of late after struggling since Cincinnati.

The two opening-day winners are set to meet on Tuesday in what should be an interesting contest, particularly given Shelton’s serving ability on the quick indoor courts.

With back-to-back titles at the Hylo Open and Kumamoto Masters Japan, the 25-year-old came out of nowhere to climb to sixth spot in the World Tour rankings and almost seal his ticket to Hangzhou, China.

However, his spot is not yet sealed, as Koki Watanabe and Kunlavut Vitidsarn are also in the race to break into the top eight and secure a place in the season finale in December.

Following his superb win over Watanabe, Sen moved ahead of the Japanese player, but it will still come down to the Hong Kong Open next week.

Lakshya has no points to defend from his runner-up finish in Hong Kong last year. Only a player’s best-14 results count, which means anything he earns in Hong Kong will replace his current lowest score of 2,220 points.

Lakshya will need to reach the semifinals in Hong Kong to be certain of his spot. However, it will also depend on how the others fare in the tournament, the final event of the qualifying window.

Lakshya opens against Lee Cheuk Yiu, while Kunlavut faces a qualifier. If both Lakshya and Kunlavut win their opening matches, they will set up a mouth-watering clash in the second round.

“Definitely that is one thing which we will be fighting for and yes, this tournament will definitely help me get good points for that as well. Now I have one more tournament, the Hong Kong Open, so now focused on that,” Lakshya said after his win on Sunday.

title: Nations Championship final round
article_text:
France and New Zealand are in pole position to qualify for the inaugural Nations Championship final heading into the last round of pool fixtures on Saturday.

England, Ireland and South Africa also have hopes of reaching the final at Allianz Stadium on 29 November.

The top-ranked team from the northern hemisphere pool will face the best team from the southern hemisphere to determine who claims the first Nations Championship title.

Scotland and Wales are also competing for fourth place in the table before the three-day finals weekend starting on Friday, 27 November.

Here is what each team needs to win their pool and the latest finals weekend fixtures as things stand.

France's outstanding 21-19 victory over world champions South Africa last Friday ensured they kept their lead in the northern group standings.

The Six Nations champions only have a one-point lead over England and Ireland, but can secure their place in the final on 29 November with a bonus-point win over Argentina at Stade de France (20:10 GMT kick-off).

A win without a bonus point might not be enough because of England's vastly superior points difference of 134 to France's 80.

Any other result and England or Ireland will look to take advantage.

England will try to beat New Zealand in the first fixture of the day (14:10) - ideally with a bonus point - to go top of the pool and put the pressure on Les Bleus before their match.

A draw or a losing bonus point would also put England top but give Ireland and France a chance to clinch the title.

Realistically, given their inferior points difference, Ireland need to not only beat the world's number one side South Africa (16:40) but also France and England to slip up.

England's superior points difference means a bonus-point win over New Zealand would realistically end Ireland's chances of making the final.

If England lose, Ireland need a big bonus-point win over South Africa and hope France fail to take maximum points against Argentina.

France's points difference of 80 compared with Ireland's 57 could come into play if they are restricted to a four-point win.

Scotland are fourth in the table - above Wales on points difference only - following a hard-fought 15-12 win over Australia on Sunday.

Wales produced the performance of the championship so far with a historic 35-28 victory over New Zealand at a raucous Principality Stadium.

Scotland welcome Japan to Murrayfield at 14:10 while Wales play Australia at 20:10.

It is not mathematically impossible for both sides to finish above Ireland but that would need the Irish to lose by a massive margin and Scotland and Wales to record huge wins to overturn the points difference.

The one thing we do know with any certainty is that Italy, who have yet to win a match, will finish bottom of the pool. They will seek to end a dismal campaign with a victory against fellow strugglers Fiji (16:40).

All Blacks or Springboks in the southern hemisphere?

New Zealand have 22 points from five games and lead South Africa by one point in the southern hemisphere pool after securing a bonus point in their shock defeat by Wales.

A bonus-point win over England will secure New Zealand's place in the final, while a four-point win should be enough given their superior points difference.

A draw or defeat at Allianz Stadium opens the door for the Springboks, who face Ireland after New Zealand play England.

Argentina claimed the only win of the fifth round for the southern hemisphere by overcoming Italy 19-15.

They have 11 points and are in a battle with Australia to finish third.

Japan will hope to overtake Australia to finish fourth but Fiji look consigned to finish bottom even if they manage a big win against Italy.

Teams earn four points for a win, two points for a draw and nothing for a loss.

Teams also have the opportunity to earn bonus points, either by scoring four or more tries and/or losing by fewer than 7 points.

The Nations Championship pits the northern hemisphere teams who compete in the Six Nations - England, Ireland, Scotland, Wales, France and Italy - against southern hemisphere giants South Africa, New Zealand, Australia and Argentina, plus invited sides Fiji and Japan.

All teams will play each of the six in the opposing hemisphere once, with three rounds of fixtures staged in July and another three in November.

Their results will rank the teams within their own hemisphere, from one to six.

On the finals weekend, there is a three-day play-off event staged at Allianz Stadium. The sixth-placed team in the northern hemisphere plays off against the equivalent in the southern hemisphere standings and so on, culminating in the two top-ranked sides taking each other on.

The winner of that final match will lift the Nations Championship trophy.

There is also a parallel, Ryder Cup-style hemisphere title. The winner of each of the play-off matches will earn one point for their hemisphere, except for the contest between the two top-ranked teams which delivers two.

The first hemisphere to earn four points over the weekend will be crowned winners.

title: Young Saints scrum-half making Goode impression
article_text:
Northampton Saints are ready to put their faith in 18-year-old Sonny Goode at scrum-half as they continue their Prem Rugby Cup campaign.

A relative novice in the role, Goode made his second first-team appearance when Jonny Weimann limped off in their 39-19 win over Leicester Tigers.

With Archie McParland on England duty, Alex Mitchell recuperating following hamstring surgery and Aidan Pugh also injured, Saints now have to rely on Goode and Fergus Mainey for the time being.

"Luckily Jonny won't be out for too long, but Sonny comes on - obviously he's been part of the under-18s set-up but not for long as a nine - and to play the game the way he did was great," coach Jake Sharp told BBC Radio Northampton.

"He's not short of confidence that kid, but the fact that he wants to get the ball, move the ball quickly and make good decisions was excellent to watch.

"He's probably played less than 10 games as a nine so that's testament to the work [under-18s head coach] Charlie Reed has done with him in the academy.

"For him to really buy into what that role is since starting training in pre-season, fair play to him."

Saints are fourth in Group B, having lost twice prior to the Leicester game, and are away to Newcastle Red Bulls on Saturday (17:30 GMT), with Goode set to make his first senior start.

"That was a really strong Leicester side... and we were really dominant in that performance across lots of aspects. The challenge for this group is consistency," added Sharp.

"The lads know what we're trying to be, and who we are from a DNA point of view, but also that they can put their own authenticity on the shirt and they are trying to be as physically dominant as they can be, I'm really proud of them."

title: 'With Sacha there’s been so much hype... I just don’t see it': England great
article_text:
Former England scrum-half Ben Youngs has questioned the hype surrounding Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu after the Springboks fly-half failed to impose himself in South Africa’s defeat to France.

Feinberg-Mngomezulu has emerged as one of the most exciting players in Test rugby over the past 18 months, but endured a frustrating evening in Paris as the Springboks fell to a 21-19 loss.

The 24-year-old struggled to take control of the contest during his 65 minutes on the field, losing possession three times and kicking one penalty dead shortly before half-time. There were flashes of his class, the clean break that led to Maxime Lucu being yellow-carded, but much of South Africa’s threat instead came through their dominant pack.

On the opposite side, Antoine Dupont was operating out of position at fly-half but still exerted the greater influence on proceedings, leaving Feinberg-Mngomezulu second best in a fascinating individual battle between two of the game’s most celebrated talents.

Speaking alongside former England and Leicester Tigers team-mate Dan Cole on the For The Love Of Rugby podcast, the 127-cap England great Youngs suggested Feinberg-Mngomezulu has yet to justify the scale of the attention surrounding him, while Cole argued South Africa’s strength elsewhere means they may not require a superstar at No.10 anyway.

Youngs said: “I feel like with Sacha, there’s been so much chat and hype around him. I just don’t see it. I don’t see it at the level that people have hyped him up at. It’s the new shiny toy and everyone’s, ‘Oh wow, it’s amazing.’

“He is when you play against Italy or a team like that, but I’ve yet to see it. Even in the Greatest Rivalry, there wasn’t a game where he dominated. There wasn’t a game where I was like, ‘Wow.’”

Cole added: “South Africa is such a well-oiled machine, you don’t need that. You just need a [Handre] Pollard who can kick his goals because your pack’s going to win you collisions, it’s going to win you set-piece penalties, and it’s going to dominate the opposition to score more tries.

“In that South Africa team, you don’t need probably a superstar at 10. The superstar, like a Pollard, basically comes from kicking his goals and doing his job.”

title: Springboks boss Rassie Erasmus launches tirade over officiating: ‘Is that not match-fixing?’

The South Africa boss Rassie Erasmus has launched an extraordinary tirade against what he perceives as unfair officiating ahead of his side’s Nations Championship clash with Ireland.

The Springboks named their side for the encounter in Dublin on Monday as they bid to bounce back from a narrow defeat to France in Paris, with Eben Etzebeth recalled.

Ireland coach Andy Farrell will confirm his selection later in the week, and could be without fly half Sam Prendergast. The 23-year-old has reportedly been cited for a hip-drop tackle on Fiji’s Peceli Yato on Saturday, though the incident was not picked up during that game.

Erasmus predicted, though, that Prendergast would be cleared of sanction by a disciplinary panel – referencing the recent decision to clear Leinster and Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong of an alleged groin grab during a game against Munster.

South African hooker Jan-Hendrik Wessels served a suspension having been found guilty of a similar accusation during a game last year, with twice World Cup-winning coach Erasmus believing it to be a case of double standards.

“We are in the northern hemisphere. I think there is going to be a technicality and he is going to play,” Erasmus said to reporters in Dublin of Prendergast.

“My experience is… like Tadhg [Furlong] got free for the same thing that Jan-Hendrik did. I don’t want to go into details there because I’m not a legal person, but from a South African point of view, that hurt, that we felt it’s more or less the same situation and Jan-Hendrik got nine weeks, the other guy got free.

“I think the hip-drop tackle was terrible, in my opinion, compared to where we were at the World Rugby meetings and all coaches were there except the Irish coach and the French coach. We had like three hours discussion about the hip-drop tackle and, you know, it’s weird.

“It’s difficult to understand when the TMO sits there and he sees that. And it was something we discussed at the World Rugby meeting, and the examples of how it is was shown over and over, and we all had input.

“Somebody sees that and he decides there’s nothing wrong with that. Then you wonder, but all of us coaches sit there and all of us gave input. So when you see that, and you decide that there’s nothing wrong with that, what do the other coaches or the other people, what did Jake [White, Fiji head coach] feel? What did that guy that got injured and got carried off?

“We all thought it’s an immediate red card. Everybody watched the game live because that’s exactly what they said the hip drop tackle is.

“I swear I’m not moaning. I’m just trying to give you a perspective of somebody who comes and play, for example, in France or in Ireland.”

Erasmus also insisted that the officials in Paris, led by referee Andrea Piardi, had missed 17 “knee-drop” tackles from France.

“Let’s say 11 of those was, I thought, at least a penalty and three I thought is at least yellow card. And not one was sanctioned. And not one was showed out or cited. And I’ll send you the playlist, but I’ll get into trouble, so I can’t send the playlist to anybody and we can only send five clips to World Rugby. So we’ll probably query it, but the answer will be, ‘Yes, it was a mistake.’ They should have penalised that

“Same with the Prendergast thing, you know, so who am I to judge that? My gut feeling is he’ll play on Saturday.”

“I’m not saying he’s wrong, I’m saying if he didn’t see it, it must be a technology problem. If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing? Is that not interfering with the outcome of a game if you see this injury that happened there, a knee-drop tackle happened there, and it’s been decided that knee drop tackles are out?

“On numerous times, we mentioned to the referee ‘we think there’s (been) a knee drop tackle’. Now, I’m saying to you, my feeling is knee drop tackles is out. They happened 17 in our games. Not one was penalised even. And if the TMO didn’t see it, maybe then technology must be better. If he saw it and he ignored it, what does that boil down to? Manipulation of the game or the result or injured players getting injured. So all I’m asking, don’t take TMOs out and discourage them to get involved. Then the wrong team will win and players will get injured. That’s all I’m saying.”

Erasmus subsequently insisted that his comments were “not an accusation”, and that he was not referring directly to his team.

“No, not us, not us,” said Erasmus. “I think Jake White’s team [Fiji], they lost their [No 8] with a hip drop tackle that was three weeks ago at the World Rugby meeting decided, over and over with clips, this is a hip drop tackle. Now all of us who were there saw it, that it’s exactly what they explained to us there. Now the TMO sees it. Now, if he didn’t see it, that’s a different thing.

“But if he saw it and he decided, ‘Well, I’m gonna ignore it.’ What would you make of it? OK, if he missed it, different story. But if he saw it and he ignored it, what is that?

title: Juan Carlos Ferrero makes ‘strange and difficult’ Carlos Alcaraz comments after ATP Finals reunion
article_text:
Juan Carlos Ferrero has described his reunion with Carlos Alcaraz ahead of the 2026 ATP Finals as “strange” and “a difficult situation.”

Alcaraz and Ferrero parted ways in December 2025, bringing an end to a hugely successful player-coach collaboration that started in 2018, when Alcaraz was 15.

While working with Ferrero, Alcaraz captured 24 ATP Tour singles titles, including six Grand Slams, and he became the youngest ATP world No 1 in history after winning his maiden major at the 2022 US Open aged 19.

In an emotional statement following the split, Ferrero suggested it was not his decision to leave Alcaraz’s team as he admitted: “I wish I could have continued.”

Earlier this month, Ferrero announced he would be returning to the ATP Tour as a member of Ben Shelton‘s coaching team.

Ferrero is in Turin for this year’s ATP Finals — where both Shelton and Alcaraz are competing.

“I have to be honest, it felt strange being on the court in front of him.

“It was a difficult situation, but as professionals we have to get used to it. He knows he’ll always be in my heart.”

Ferrero also discussed his experience of working with Shelton so far.

title: Frances Tiafoe states what he found ‘kind of weird’ about playing Carlos Alcaraz at the ATP Finals
article_text:
Frances Tiafoe’s first-ever experience of the ATP Finals ended with a gruelling defeat at the hands of Carlos Alcaraz.

The American qualified at the world No 8 this season to mark his first appearance at the year-end tournament, but his first match ended 6-2, 6-2 in favour of Alcaraz in just over an hour.

Alcaraz was absolutely superb throughout, and even hit a performance rating of 9.6, but Tiafoe looked like a deer in the headlights for much of the contest.

Despite his gruelling defeat, Tiafoe cut an upbeat figure in his post-match press conferences, where he was asked about his difficulties on the court.

“It was fun, about the whole hour of it, was a lot of fun,” said Tiafoe about his first-ever experience of the ATP Finals.

“But yeah, I mean, it’s a great experience to be out here. The walkout is super special. It’s an experience I haven’t had,” continued the American.

He did admit, however, that it was a different experience to play a player of Alcaraz’s quality in the first match of a tournament.

“It’s kind of weird coming out and play your first match against him. Normally play him deep in the draw. It’s cool. It was a cool experience,” said Tiafoe.

“This tournament is super well done from everything: own lockers, the walkout, the food. Everything is pretty special. Having your own security, it’s cool. Yeah, I mean, he has moments where he’s definitely Superman and he’s playing pretty insane.

“But again, it’s one of those things, yeah, you got to definitely appreciate greatness. I’m one who appreciates greatness. But at the same time, like, he played great, but I’m not one to put someone totally on a pedestal.

“I mean, I will give respect where it’s due, but I don’t want to just keep saying how great he is. Eventually someone’s got to beat him.”

Tiafoe has two more chances at the ATP Finals, with the round robin format at the year-end tournament.

He will likely need to win both of those matches to give himself a chance of qualifying for the knockout stages, due to the straight sets defeat to Alcaraz.

Tiafoe will play Daniil Medvedev and Flavio Cobolli at the ATP Finals to keep his hopes of qualifying for the latter stages.

Those two men are set to play in the evening session on Monday, 16th November, and Tiafoe will likely be hoping either will win by a straight sets scoreline.

Tiafoe has a difficult record against Medvedev, but his head-to-head record against Cobolli is far more successful.

He has lost six of his eight matches to the Russian star, whereas he leads his head-to-head against Cobolli with four victories from five matches.

title: Carlos Alcaraz asked if he feels ‘unstoppable’ after destroying Frances Tiafoe at ATP Finals
article_text:
Carlos Alcaraz began his campaign at the 2026 ATP Finals in style by delivering a masterclass to dismantle Frances Tiafoe.

World No 3 Alcaraz crushed eighth-ranked Tiafoe 6-2, 6-2 in his opening match in the John McEnroe Group in Turin on Monday.

Alcaraz won 57 of the 93 points (61%) and recorded 21 winners to just nine unforced errors, while he won all 12 of the points on Tiafoe’s second serve.

The seven-time Grand Slam champion registered an ATP Tennis Insights performance rating of 9.6/10 — the second-highest score recorded in his career.

In his post-match press conference, Alcaraz was asked if he feels “unstoppable” when he is in the type of form he showcased against Tiafoe.

“Well, not that feeling, to be honest,” said the Spaniard.

“But I feel like sometimes, I feel really comfortable, you know, in every aspect of the game.

“I feel like I’m better than the opponent in every aspect of the game. It could be like that, but in my mind, I just feel that way.

“When I return every serve, when I feel like he doesn’t get in that much of my game, I just go with the flow all the time.

“So, I think just when I get that feeling, everything goes pretty well.”

Alcaraz was also asked if this year’s ATP Finals feels more special than his previous appearances at the event given his lengthy injury absence this season.

“No, I didn’t feel it was special or it was more special than others,” he replied.

“Obviously, playing here is always a privilege. It’s special qualifying, playing with the best, having such an amazing week.

“If I qualify to the semi-final or not, I think it’s a great experience, a great week, getting experience, you know, every year that I played here.

“But no, it’s been a really different year for me, but, you know, coming here and playing this match, it wasn’t more special than others.”

Alcaraz will play Daniil Medvedev and Flavio Cobolli in his remaining round robin matches in Turin.

The 23-year-old is aiming to win his maiden title at the ATP Finals, having been a runner-up at last year’s edition.

title: Don't fall for this common golf setup myth, says top teacher
article_text:
Ask ten golfers on the range what they’re thinking about at address and you’ll likely get ten different answers: Keep your head down. Bend 45 degrees at the hips. Square your feet. Keep your left arm rigid.

We’ve been conditioned to view the golf setup as a static checklist of rules — a rigid pose designed simply to hold us in place before the action begins. That mindset is one of the biggest reasons golfers struggle with consistency.

The setup shouldn’t be viewed as a static posture. Rather, it’s the launchpad for a dynamic motion.

Every golf swing begins with a specific objective, whether that’s a particular ball flight, trajectory, curve or feel. Your address position should reflect that objective. If the way you set up doesn’t support the shot you’re trying to hit, you’re making the swing harder before it even begins. Simply put: Your setup must match your intent.

One of the biggest myths in golf instruction is that there’s a single, perfect setup that works for every shot and every golfer.

Think about it: Would you use the same address position, ball position and spine tilt to hit a high, soft draw over a tree that you would to hit a low, piercing stinger into the wind? Of course not. Yet golfers often approach every shot with essentially the same setup.

When your setup says, I’m going to hit a low, straight shot, but your intention is to launch the ball high over a bunker, you’re creating a conflict between your physical position and your athletic objective. Your body will naturally try to find a way to produce the shot you’re envisioning, often leading to last-second adjustments and compensations during the swing.

The problem isn’t necessarily your downswing. It’s that your setup and your intention aren’t working together.

The next time you play, try flipping your approach to address. Rather than defaulting to a standard setup and hoping it works for the shot in front of you, build your address position around what you’re trying to accomplish.

1. Define your intent: Stand behind the ball and visualize the shot you want to hit. Picture its trajectory, shape and landing area.

2. Build your setup: Step up to the ball and adjust your posture, spine angle, foot position and ball position to support the shot you’ve envisioned.

3. Trust your motion: Once your setup matches your intent, stop worrying about individual positions and let your natural athleticism take over.

Your setup should never be something you simply fall into out of habit. It should be a deliberate part of your shot-making process. When your address position supports what you’re trying to accomplish, you eliminate unnecessary conflict and give yourself a much better chance of delivering the club the way you intend.

title: Lakshya aims to seal BWF World Tour final spot at Hong Kong Open
article_text:
India’s Lakshya Sen will aim to continue his rampaging run, go deep into the draw and seal his place in the season-ending BWF World Tour Finals when he begins his campaign at the Hong Kong Super 500 starting on Tuesday.

With back-to-back titles at the Hylo Open and Kumamoto Masters Japan, the 25-year-old came out of nowhere to climb to sixth spot in the World Tour rankings and almost seal his ticket to Hangzhou, China.

However, his spot is not yet sealed, as Koki Watanabe and Kunlavut Vitidsarn are also in the race to break into the top eight and secure a place in the season finale in December.

Following his superb win over Watanabe, Sen moved ahead of the Japanese player, but it will still come down to the Hong Kong Open next week.

Lakshya has no points to defend from his runner-up finish in Hong Kong last year. Only a player’s best-14 results count, which means anything he earns in Hong Kong will replace his current lowest score of 2,220 points.

Lakshya will need to reach the semifinals in Hong Kong to be certain of his spot. However, it will also depend on how the others fare in the tournament, the final event of the qualifying window.

Lakshya opens against Lee Cheuk Yiu, while Kunlavut faces a qualifier. If both Lakshya and Kunlavut win their opening matches, they will set up a mouth-watering clash in the second round.

Watanabe is in the other half of the draw and will start against compatriot Kenta Nishimoto, meaning he can meet either of them only in the final.

“Definitely that is one thing which we will be fighting for and yes, this tournament will definitely help me get good points for that as well. Now I have one more tournament, the Hong Kong Open, so now focused on that,” Lakshya said after his win on Sunday.

Among other Indians, Kidambi Srikanth will meet seventh seed Alwi Farhan, who has already sealed his place in the season finale.

There will be a host of young Indian players in the women’s singles, with Anmol Kharb facing Japan’s fourth seed Tomoka Miyazaki, Unnati Hooda taking on eighth seed Han Yue, and compatriots Ashmita Chaliha and Isharani Baruah facing each other in their opening match.

Devika Sihag will meet Lin Hsiang Ti of Chinese Taipei, while Rakshita Ramraj will square off against Denmark’s Mia Blichfeldt.

In men’s doubles, world No. 6 Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty, seeded fifth, are scheduled to face China’s Hu Ke Yuan and Lin Xiang Yi, while Hariharan Amsakarunan and MR Arjun will open against a qualifier.

World Championships bronze medallists Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand will face a qualifying pair in women’s doubles.

In mixed doubles, Hariharan and Tanisha Crasto will take on Malaysia’s Wong Tien Ci and Lim Chiew Sien, while Dhruv Rawat and Maneesha K will open against China’s second seeds Jiang Zhen Bang and Wei Ya Xin.

title: Sunshine Stars partner firm for sponsorship deal

title: Australian media watchdog presses TV networks to curb sports alcohol ads
article_text:
Australia’s media regulator has called on the free-to-air TV sector to take “immediate steps” to lower children’s exposure to alcohol ads and remove exemptions allowing them to be shown during sports broadcasts.

Under current rules, direct alcohol adverts on terrestrial free-to-air television are restricted to overnight hours, from 8:30 pm to 5:00 am, and a midday window, from 12:00 pm to 3:00 pm on school days.

Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.

However, exemptions apply to sports programmes broadcast on weekends and public holidays, as well as qualifying live sports broadcasts shown across multiple markets.

The Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) has recommended that industry body Free TV Australia remove those exemptions.

ACMA chair Nerida O’Loughlin said: “These exemptions are unique to Australia and inconsistent with advertising of other restricted products, such as gambling.”

The media watchdog began a review in March to assess whether the existing rules provide “appropriate community safeguards” for television audiences.

It said its review found “widespread concern” about alcohol advertising and recognised a link between such advertising, increased consumption, and “risky drinking”.

The review also found that alcohol advertising on television represents a “relatively small” but “important” source of revenue for broadcasters.

The ACMA has also asked Free TV Australia to “voluntarily apply” the Free TV Code to television content provided through broadcasters’ online services.

If Free TV Australia does not submit a revised code for registration that provides appropriate community safeguards, the ACMA could determine a programme standard, it said.

Separate standards prohibit alcohol advertising before, during, and after children’s programmes. Cross-media industry codes also require adverts shown without age-gating to reach audiences expected to comprise at least 80% adults.

The ACMA has recommended that the Australian Government conduct a “holistic review” of alcohol advertising across all media.

“Our review found strong concerns about exposure to alcohol advertising through other media including online, at sporting venues, on jerseys and in other forms that all fall outside the ACMA’s remit.

“As a result, the ACMA has recommended that the Australian Government consider alcohol advertising regulation holistically, including looking at potential gaps and inconsistencies across platforms,” O’Loughlin said.

title: Nations Championship: England's Will Joseph in line to start against New Zealand
article_text:
England's Will Joseph is in line to retain his place for Saturday's blockbuster Nations Championship meeting with New Zealand after scoring five tries against Japan.

In the absence of the injured Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, Joseph is understood to be in pole position to reprise his role on the wing after a performance packed with pace and finishing ability.

Joseph scored a hat-trick inside the first 19 minutes, on the way to becoming only the fifth England men's player to score five tries in one match.

He also headed the team's charts for metres carried (224) and top speed (21.7mph).

The 24-year-old won his second Test cap in Saturday's 78-15 thrashing of the Brave Blossoms, four and half years after making his debut as a teenager.

After a late cameo as a replacement in England's second Test win over Australia in July 2022, Joseph struggled to fulfil his promise. Boyhood club London Irish went into liquidation and a stint at Harlequins was hampered by injury and a lack of game time.

However, Joseph has been a key part of Gloucester's resurgence this season and, watched by elder brother and former England centre Jonathan Joseph, he made a sensational return to international rugby at Allianz Stadium last weekend.

"He is just so fast. He doesn't look too fast in the first two steps and then he is just gone. He gets away from people," said former England wing Chris Ashton on BBC Radio 5 Live of Joseph's ability.

"He floats, doesn't he?" added England team-mate Ben Earl to BBC Sport.

"The way he carries himself, he does really move like his brother. They are so, so similar."

With Feyi-Waboso ruled out of the autumn by an ankle injury, Cadan Murley is the other specialist wing in England's squad vying with Joseph for a spot alongside likely first-choice Tommy Freeman in the back three.

After victories over Australia and Japan this autumn, England are second in the Nations Championship northern hemisphere standings and in line for a play-off meeting with South Africa on finals weekend on 27-29 November.

However, that could change considerably, with New Zealand leading the southern hemisphere table and second-place South Africa taking on Ireland, who are behind England only on points difference.

title: India women clinch bronze in U20 rugby sevens meet
article_text:
BHUBANESWAR: Fresh from their victory over the New Zealand women’s U20 invitational side during the India-New Zealand Rugby Series in Rajgir, Bihar, last month, the Indian women’s U20 team secured the bronze medal at Asia Rugby U20 Sevens at Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar on Sunday.

The hosts defeated Sri Lanka 27-0 to finish on the podium for the second consecutive year.

After winning all three of their matches on Saturday, the team coached by Kiano Fourie went down to Malaysia 12-14 in a closely contested semifinal. Samruddhi Kadam and Khushi Devi scored a try each, while Mamali Singh added a conversion as India pushed Malaysia throughout the contest before the visitors edged through to the final.

The hosts, however, bounced back strongly in the bronze-medal match against Sri Lanka, registering a comprehensive 27-0 victory. Samruddhi scored two tries, while Aditi Londhe, Akshaya NS and Anita Murmu added one try each. Dipali Tathe also contributed with a conversion.

The victory ensured India finished third for the second consecutive year, following their bronze-medal finish at the previous edition in Rajgir.

However, it was not a happy outing for the Indian men’s U20 team.

After recording two wins from three matches on Saturday, India lost 5-12 to Chinese Taipei in their final group-stage fixture, with Rahul Majhi scoring the hosts’ only try. In their next outing against Singapore, India suffered a 5-29 defeat, with Rahul again getting on the scoresheet.

India, though, concluded its campaign on a positive note with a 24-7 victory over Thailand in the seventh/eighth-place playoff. Ajit Nag scored two tries, while Pushpender and Naman Yadav added one each. Bharat Kisan and Rahul contributed a conversion apiece to help India secure seventh place overall.

Hong Kong China, meanwhile, emerged champions in both the men’s and women’s categories, with Malaysia finishing runners-up in both competitions. Chinese Taipei claimed third place in the men’s category.

title: Lewis Moody's touching tribute to sons as he reveals health update and next challenge
article_text:
Lewis Moody paid a heartfelt tribute to his sons for the way they have handled his motor neuron disease diagnosis as he unveiled his next charity challenge.

The England World Cup winger was diagnosed with MND in September last year, prompting him to link up with the My Name'5 Doddie Foundation, launched in memory of Scottish rugby legend Doddie Weir, who died from the life-limiting condition in 2022, aged 52.

Moody has revealed his latest charity challenge, Front Up: Walk the Coast, which is inviting thousands of people across the UK to walk 26 miles along one of more than 175 routes on June 12 next year, the day of his 49th birthday.

It is Moody's second major fundraising endeavour, following a 500-mile bike ride from Newcastle to Twickenham in June, which raised over £600,000. He was joined on the ride by a host of rugby friends and legends, including Martin Johnson, Jonny Wilkinson and Kenny Logan.

Moody's wife Annie and sons Dylan and Ethan also took part and will be involved again in Walk the Coast. He brought up his sons when asked about his proudest moment of the last year.
